subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Cardin:
That a special committee of this House, consisting of nine members, be appointed forthwith to investigate the administration of the Department of Customs and Excise and alleged serious losses to the public treasury because of inefficiency or corruption on the part of officers of the department and others, and that such investigation extend back over such period of time as the committee may decide and have regard to all matters affecting the prevention of smuggling, the prosecution of offenders, the seizure, storage and disposal of smuggled goods, or goods seized for the purposes of excise or other taxes, the appraisal of goods for revenue purposes, the collection of customs and excise duties, the knowledge of ministers or officials of offences or irregularities affecting the public service in said department, the efficiency of the administration thereof, and the necessity of safeguarding the public revenue and the public treasury, and that such committee have power to send for persons, papers and records, to adjourn from place to place, to print the evidence taken before the committee, and to report from time to time.
I do not intend to offer any extended remarks in connection with the motion. I only desire to thank the right hon. leader of the opposition, and also the hon. member for
Customs Inquiry Committee

Battle River (Mr. Spencer), for the courtesies extended to me in connection with the drafting of the motion and during the negotiations which took place between us concerning the motion which is now before the House.

It places the membership representing the government benches on an equality with the membership representing these benches, notwithstanding the fact that we have a substantially larger number in the House. I want to make mention of another feature. It was thought, and in this there was no divergence of view, that there should not be restriction upon the committee as to the period over which it might view the Customs department's administration. While the charges are confined to a comparatively limited period1 of time, it is. quite manifest that files may relate back over some considerable period, and that it would be unfair to restrain the committee in respect of time. I know the country will expect, and we will all expect, that the committee will not use this liberty 
to dissipate its energies and to spread thinly over a tremendous period an investigation, which must necessarily be deep and thorough as to the actual facts that are now in question.

The duties of the Speaker are sometimes rather arduous and when matters such as this arise I rely upon Hatsell, a famous authority on the rules and procedure of the House of Commons. I read the following passage for the information of the hon. members:
It is impossible to lay down any specific rules upon this point, or to declare before-hand what expressions are or are not contrary to order; so much depends upon the tone, and manner, and intention of the person speaking-something upon the person to whom they are addressed, whether a minister in a responsible station, or a private member not in office; - whether the words are meant to be applied to his public coonduct, or to his private character;-the degree of provocation which the member speaking had received from the person he alludes to: all these considerations must be attended to at the moment, as they are infinitely various, and cannot possibly be foreseen in such a manner as that precise rules can be adopted with respect to them.
It is therefore rather difficult for me to say whether the intent of the hon. member in using a rather strong and strange expression was to introduce language of a scurrilous or insulting nature. Yesterday I did not find in the expression of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard anything which constituted an attack upon the character of any of his fellow members in the House. The expression appears to have been the hon. member's way of characterizing the attitude of the party to my right. I appeal to the good sense of the House to be as gentle as possible in the use of such expressions during debate.

Mr. Speaker, before I sit down, I intend to move an amendment to the amendment of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), carrying out the arrangement made in regard to the alteration of thait amendment in connection with the Department of Customs. But before doing so, I would like to say a few words regarding the motion now before the House and proposed by the government for a lengthy adjournment, and to give some reasons why I think it should not carry. Has anyone ever seen a spectacle such as this since parliamentary government came into being in British countries? The government was in power for four years; it had a majority of one of its members, and it carried on during those four years with the co-operation of the Progressive party. Was the government thankful for that co-operation? Certainly not. No one can put this more strongly than my hon. friend the lady member of this House (Miss MacPhail), who criticised the Prime Minister for exhibiting an utter lack of gratitude or graciousness towards that party. Did they translate into legislation during those four years any of the policies that are specially dear to my hon. friends to my left? Certainly not. They Chose their own time for a general election. The Prime Minister went to Richmond Hill where he delivered a speech, carefully prepared, stating his reasons for going to the country, and I want to quote a couple of statements he made at that time. Mr. King said:
Is it sufficient that as a government we should continue in office, drawing our indemnities and salaries as members and ministers and enjoying the other fruits of office, when great national questions press for solution with which, for want of an adequate majority in parliament, we are unable satisfactorily to cope?

A very good reason, in my judgment, and in the judigment of the people for going to the country. Then 'he went on to say:
May I say further. ... I do not believe any one of the four-
That is the important questions to be dealt
with.
-can be dealt with effectively at a last session of parliament. They can only be satisfactorily dealt with by a House of Commons fresh from the people and with a mandate from the people to carry out their will.
I would say further, I do not believe that any one of the four can be dealt with effectively by a government which is not supported by a substantial majority in the House of Commons. Group government and minority government may be inevitable in transitional phases of our political history, but neither is the kind of government wherewith to achieve great reforms.
In other words, he was not satisfied with a majority of one to carry on with the support of the Progressive party in this House. The election took pflace. and after the election the government stilll claim their right to cany on, although 'they came 'back into this House with a minority, the remnant of a government or committee of parliament. So this House met, and on a division this government was sustained, first, by a meagre majority of three, then by a majority of -ten, and finally the other evening by a majority of one. After claiming the right in this way to retain power, although being in a minority in this country and in this House, and after being supported in the way I have mentioned on a division, they bring in this motion for a lengthy adjournment. To me the two things are utterly inconsistent. Either they should not be here claiming to be a government, or they should carry on. Why have they asked for this 'adjournment? For the simple and only reason that they cannot carry on as they are. 'Is it any wonder that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) thought it best not Ito rise the other day to make any remarks in support of this motion far an adjournment? I am not at alii surprised that he did not rise to speak, because he had no real reason to give for an adjournment except the inability of the government to function. When 'he was finally forced to rise in his seat the day before yesterday, what did he say in explanation of this request for an adjournment? He said:
These changes must be made by the present Prime Minister and he asks an adjournment for that purpose. I think it would be only fair on the part of my right hon. friend and of hon. gentlemen opposite to grant what is certainly a reasonable request.
In other words, he calmly tells this House: "We cannot carry on as we are. Let us go away for six weeks and we will try to repair the government and to put it into such 14011-50
shape that it can carry on." In this statement it seems to me the Minister of Justice gives his whole case away. There is no real public reason why this adjournment should be agreed to. The minister referred to what he called precedents for his action in this matter. He referred to the case of 1911 when Sir Wilfrid Laurier went to England and when, with the consent of both parties, an adjournment of this House was agreed to for the purpose of allowing him to proceed to London. My hon. friend had better be careful of these lengthy adjournments taken by Liberal governments, because that one did not end very satisfactorily to hon. gentlemen opposite. I remember very well the occasion on which it was granted in this House, the time when the reciprocity pact was up for discussion. In the result, when the adjournment was over, the government came back into this House and found that the country was against them. They had an election and they were defeated and left at home. Therefore, my hon. friend had better be careful about precedents such as that of 1911. In 1917, the situation was entirely different. We are all agreed that the business of this country should be attended to and that is one reason why we want to have this House continue in session, but in 1917 there had to be attended to in London a matter which was very important for this country. We were in the midst of the Great war and a call had come from London for the meeting of the first imperial war cabinet, when the representatives of the various dominions sat around the table in perfect equality with the representatives of the Mother Country to discuss the numerous phases of the war and the many troublesome problems Which had to be decided at that critical time. I say therefore that the reason for that adjournment was one to which no one could take any objection, and one which we hope may never occur again. It seems to me that neither of the precedents cited applies to this particular case. The Minister of Justice made his ease as strong as he could but there is nothing that can be said to bolster it up.
Then I come to some other reasons why we object to this adjournment. The least important consideration is the convenience to members of this House, and I mention this fact as one of those to whom it would 'be least inconvenient, inasmuch as I live jn the city of Ottawa. But it appeals to me strongly as most unfair and unreasonable to bring members from all parts of Canada to this city and send them away after a session of two or three weeks. They are sufficiently inconvenienced

Lest some one should make the remark afterwards, Mr. Speaker, I want to say: Let no one suggest that in this ease a similar difficulty is unlikely to arise. It is the very thing we must be prepared to meet. If scoundrels and unscrupulous business men are involved in this investigation, 'as no doubt they will be, they certainly will! stop at nothing to -try to prevent the facts -being brought to light; in other words, they will make every effort to avoid incriminating themselves. Therefore it seems to me that fo-r the honour and dignity of this House we should not grant the long adjournment asked for by the government, but that on the contrary the House should continue in session in order that it may deal with any recalcitrant witnesses.
For these various reasons, Mr. Speaker, I am definitely opposed to the granting of this lengthy adjournment, I say to hon. gentlemen opposite, that in my opinion, if they wish to -remain in power and to retain the respect of the people of this country, they dare not -press -their motion for a lengthy adjournment at this critical time. I agree entirely with what the hon. member has said in go far as the powers of the committee and those of the House are concerned. It must be remembered however, that the inquiry will be so thorough and will extend back over so long a period of time that it will be absolutely impossible to have it completed within the short period of four weeks. For that reason, when the subpoenas are issued, if any witness refuses to obey the order and does not appear before the committee, or if any witness appearing before the committee refuses to answer legitimate questions, it will be quite possible and quite feasible to take up the .examination of other witnesses and appeal for a ruling to the House when it resumes its sittings on or after the 15th day of March. The argument that the House must be kept jn session in order to act as a court of appeal to force witnesses to answer questions, is well worthy of consideration, but it is not an argument sufficiently strong to defeat the motion under debate nor to weigh against the many arguments that the hon. leader of the House gave the other day in favour of an adjournment.
Let me once more assure my hon. friends that in so far as we are concerned, we desire to make the inquiry thorough, and we have no objection to begin the inquiry as soon as possible. It is true that the words "scoundrels" and "dishonest men" were used by the hon. member for Argenteuil. Some-of the witnesses may be scoundrels and dishonest men but I still have faith enough in my country to believe that among the witnesses called there will be enough honest men to keep the committee at work for a period of at least four weeks.

It as true that if these witnesses refuse to answer w'e can commit them to gaol only until the close of the session; but I expect to see the county gaol of Carleton filled with them while this committee is functioning, and I hope by the dose of the session this committee will have elicited such information as will enable the Minister of Customs to carry out his pledge to this House, to place them under criminal indictment and so take care of them for many years in the penitentiaries of this country. I wish to say one word to hon. gentlemen who are on my left. I came to this House with a feeling that the Progressive group occupied an entirely independent position here. Being convinced of that, I have stated,

I have before me the returns of the last Dominion election. It shows that 1,467,596 voters in the Dominion voted for the Conservative party. Against that, there were 1,689,975 who voted on the opposite side.

What did he base his statement upon? It was based upon an investigation which was carried on by this .government for the purpose of prosecuting those who had been engaged in smuggling in this country. That is what the hon. gentleman based his statement upon, coupled with newspaper reports of court proceedings. He did not offer anything new, and when the committee was accepted this afternoon hon. gentlemen opposite resumed their opposition to the adjournment for no other reason than to embarrass the government and thereby obstruct the business of the country. What is the object of their new amendment? They know that there will be an adjournment and they also know that every day the adjournment is delayed the business of the House is retarded to that extent. My hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Cahan) was apprehensive of what might happen during the interval of the adjournment. But surely it must occur to him that before the committee could start to function properly, before it would be well organized, the House would be in session again. Be honest anyway.

My hon. friend from West Calgary says, "be honest anyway." That is good advice for the hon. gentleman to follow and I shall probably have some reference to make to that later on.

This talk of smuggling, of the abuses of the customs tariff, is largely the product and the outgrowth of the legislation of the Union government. You will remember, Sir, that we had a union of the political office-seekers, the political recanters, the political uplifters and the political-
Patriots.

Yes, that is a good word my hon. friend suggests. The so-called patriots of those days, the political faddists- every one of the different elements of that union had to have its special legislation. The uplifters had to have prohibition; the faddists had to have a Civil Service Commission; the unionists among them, or politicians, had to have the fieshpots. They brought about one Sunday morning in this House the great prohibition legislation that the country has been suffering from ever since. I say, "suffering from" advisedly, Sir. When prohibition was enacted in the way it was, it made criminals of a class of people who had been in the liquor trade for generations, people who had been engaged in an honest industry for generations, and overnight they were told they were criminals. These men were not of the ordinary criminal class that could be held in check by the regular police force. They were a brand new set of people who were accepted in good society everywhere-the people who had been engaged in the liquor traffic of the country- and when that legislation put them out of business they went into the illicit handling of liquor to a large extent, and they followed that up by going into the illicit handling of other goods from across the border. When the government found themselves faced with this brand new condition, a condition in which people of all walks of life were more or less active in illicit business, it became evident that a special police force would be necessary to meet it. The government came to the House for the requisite authority, but they were met by the Civil Service Commission. My hon. friends opposite argued that the Civil Service Commission was the competent body to select men for the special police force to curb this illicit traffic. My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition only a day or two ago said that the action of the government was a political move designed to take the appointments out of the hands of the Civil Service Commission
This condition of affairs has been going on for more than five or six years, and I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that it will continue, and that it will take more than a special committee of this House to stop it. It will take

speechtext:
I think the House will agree with me when I say that it is impossible to satisfy hon. gentlemen opposite in regard to any matter. When the proposition for an adjournment was made my hon. friends opposite discussed every question under heaven but the point as to whether, in the interests of the whole country, it was not wise and proper that the government, having received a vote of confidence from the House, should be given an opportunity to fill
up its membership. We were denounced as being cripples, and as being this, that, and everything else. Then the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) comes on the scene, and in a speech of fierce invective charges maladministration on the part of the customs service in this country. That speech was most interesting to listen to and covered a great deal of ground. But the whole pith of his utterances was that this government was responsible for certain doings by certain customs officials, and he laboured with the greatest possible energy all these questions, particularly the Giroux case. I would ask the House to look at page 689 of Hansard, where my hon. friend proceeded to deal with what he called the Giroux case. With the aid of all kinds of arguments and adjectives he sought to convince the House that certain drugs which had been taken and placed in the custody of certain officials of Montreal had been stolen. In addition to that, he went on to tell us the story of the murders that had taken place down there, as if the officials of this government were in some way mixed up with those occurrences. I want to tell him that the incident to which he refers took place in December, 1920, when the Conservative party was in power. I want to reiterate that statement in the hearing of the members in this House, and to assert that when the hon. member for Vancouver Centre was proceeding to discuss this question in regard to this particular incident, alleging that some official under the Liberal party, since we came into power in 1921, was responsible for that occurrence, he either knew the statement was wrong when he made it and was misleading the House, or he did not know the true facts, because that incident took place in Montreal in December, 1920, when my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) was in power.
Now, having nothing to fear, my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin) comes to this House and says, "We are prepared to grant a committee to examine into every phase of the Customs department, not merely for four years, but for as long a period as you want to go back." He confers with my right hon. friend, prepares a resolution and brings it to the House giving the committee the widest powers to deal with the whole matter. Then my hon. friends go on to say, "Oh but you cannot adjourn now, because this committee cannot function properly when the House is not sitting." Well, my hon. friend who made that argument and the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) know very well that whether the House was in session or not, if a witness refused to obey

Adjournment-Customs Inquiry
the direction of the committee or to attend, all we could do would be to put him in charge of the Sergeant-at-Arms until this House rose. Under the law as it stands at present, and as is has always stood, there is no provision on the statute book by which parliament is empowered to do anything more than restrain the liberty of the individual during the time the House is in session.

In the case which I cited,
was it not made clear that parliament had a right to arrest, through the Sergeant-at-Arms, and had the power to commit to the county gaol during the session of parliament?

That is exactly what I said. The
power of parliament was limited to restraining the liberty of the individual while parliament was in session but not beyond that. I was in the House of Commons at the time of the Miller case, and we all felt the farcical nature of the powers of the Commons. There will have to be a statute passed-and it could be passed-conferring power on the Sergeant-at-Arms in certain cases before you can have any control over witnesses who refuse to answer or who refuse to appear. My hon. friends say, "You cannot adjourn now, because if you do this committee cannot function." The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, spoke of the great criminal lawyers in the province of Quebec and stated that these men would retain these great lawyers. Are there not great lawyers who can be obtained to prosecute for the government and the people of the country? Does my hon. friend think that the government does not propose that counsel of the first rank shall be retained to see that this matter is delved into and investigated to the bottom, and that these cases which have been held up, before the House and the country, as having occurred under our administration, as well as in previous years, shall be fully investigated and placed before the public?

If, as the hon. minister
says our powers of punishment are now too light and we need a statute to make them more drastic, would it not be well to stay here and pass such a statute?

You cannot satisfy my hon. friends.
We are here and they are there. And they are very anxious to be here. That is the whole sum and substance of the talk.

That is not quite an
answer.

My hon. friend says the committee
will be sitting and hon. members will not be able to attend that committee. I would like to know what all the hon. members who come to this House representing their constituencies are going to do when this committee is appointed and is holding sessions. Are they all going to crowd into the committee room to hear the evidence? I venture to think every wise member who wants to form a judgment as to what evidence has been presented will read the proceedings of the committee printed, as they will be, from day to day under the usual practice. My hon. friend would think this committee was going to get through its work in three weeks. It will be sitting for three months and probably more.
As bad as that?

And my hon. friend will find that there are stories other than those told by the hon.'member for Vancouver Centre, and that there are other incidents which occurred previous to 1621 which will see the light of day and which are of quite as much importance and interest to the country as any incident my hon. friend discloses. I say that every hon. member who wants to follow the proceedings of this committee will look at the printed proceedings and study them, in order that he may know exactly what occurs. He is going to do that anyway if he is interested in the matter. But look at the one hundred and one other matters of importance that hon. members are sent here to deal with. Are all these to be forgotten and excluded from consideration, except this one subject of attendance upon the committee? The arguments of my hon. friends have no virtue so far as strength and virility are concerned, when you examine them. There are the facts. The power of the committee of parliament is just as great and just as limited as it ever was. The committee will take some days at least for organization, employment of counsel, preparation of documents, and the airangement of all these details which every hon. member who has had experience in investigating knows about. The hon. members who have not had any experience in investigating committees may be apt to be misled by specious theories that you are going to start off to-morrow with filing of documents and hearing of witnesses and so on. A wide inquiry must be made in order to be effective. I say that this committee can meet and it has the control of its own destinies. Counsel will be employed to function with it and it will proceed in the

Adjournment-Customs Inquiry
regular way. But constituted as we are in this House there is no use in hon. members iterating and reiterating that they have 116 men on that side of the House, while we have only 110 on this side, and that there are certain independent gentlemen in the House. We all know' that. Why not look the facts straight in the face? We have been sustained by a majority of the House. This government desires to go on and function with the support of the House so long as it can secure that, just as any other government would do. In order to carry on, we want to fill up the portfolios. Is that an unreasonable request to make of the House or of the people, who, I am sure, if the House extends us its confidence in this respect, will justify that confidence? The public business will go on. The adjournment will not be for such a long period if we put it to the day fixed by the resolution. The government will then come to this House with its cabinet completed and be prepared to go on, not merely with the investigation of the Customs department, but with the transaction of the public business in the best interest of the Canadian people.
